title: Cash Flow Stretch Adventure
welcome_lead: Exam-style stretch. Evaluate solutions to a cash crisis and judge a forecast's reliability.

final_note: You can evaluate cash-flow solutions, judge a forecast's reliability and recommend with reasoning.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Compare cost vs speed vs side-effects.

Overdrafts: fast but interest. Factoring: instant cash but you receive less. Cutting marketing: cheap but hurts future sales.

Forecasts are predictions — and can be wrong.

They depend on assumed sales, costs, and timing. New firms have especially unreliable forecasts.

Quote the figures, explain the knock-on effects across months, then recommend a remedy that suits the business.

Avoid generic advice — match the action to the actual cause of the cash gap.

mcqs.q: Why can a profitable business still fail?
options: If a business is profitable it cannot run out of money.
Profitable businesses fail only when employees steal.
Cash flow only matters at year-end.
Because cash flow and profit are different — a business may be profitable on paper but run out of cash to pay bills, especially if customers owe money or stock ties up funds.

mcqs.q: Why are cash flow and profit different on different time-scales?
options: Cash flow and profit are the same thing measured differently.
Cash flow only matters at year-end.
Profitable businesses fail only when employees steal.

Profit is recognised when a sale is made (even on credit); cash flow is when money actually moves. A profitable sale today may produce no cash for 60 days while bills are due — creating a cash-flow problem despite profit.
Limited liability means a business can only operate for a limited time.
Cash flow only matters at year-end.
Limited liability means the company has limited debts it can take on.
Shareholders' personal assets are protected if the company fails — they can only lose the amount they invested, not their personal wealth.
